{{nihongo|'''San Marino Shrine'''|サンマリノ神社|San Marino Jinja|lead=yes}} is a shrine in [[Serravalle, San Marino|Serravalle]], [[San Marino|Republic of San Marino]]. It is the first official Shinto shrine in Europe supported by the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]] when the shrine was established.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SAN MARINO JINJA |url=https://www.sanmarinojinja.com/en/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160527102224/http://www.sanmarino-jinja.com/en/ |url-status=usurped |archive-date=May 27, 2016 |access-date=2023-10-15 |website=San Marino Jinja |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=SHRINE |url=https://www.sanmarinojinja.com/en/shrine/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430224629/https://www.sanmarinojinja.com/en/shrine/ |url-status=usurped |archive-date=April 30, 2019 |access-date=2023-10-15 |website=San Marino Jinja |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2016-08-01 |title=The curious case of San Marino |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2016/08/01/the-curious-case-of-san-marino/ |access-date=2023-10-15 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== History ==
{{ill|Manlio Cadero|ja|マンリオ・カデロ}} planned the construction of the shrine in consultation with the Jinja Honcho. It was financed through the sale of 'Japan-San Marino Friendship Charity Gold Coins'.<ref>{{Cite web |date=18 January 2013 |title=国民運動 « 日本会議 |url=https://www.nipponkaigi.org/activity/page/12 |access-date=2024-01-21 |website=www.nipponkaigi.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=May 2013 |title=日本の息吹 |work=[[Nippon Kaigi]]}}</ref>

The shrine was founded on 21 June 2014, and opened to the public the following day. The San Marino shrine was inaugurated in the presence of 150 personalities including the president of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]] and [[Yōko Abe|Yoko Kishi]], mother of the former Prime Minister of Japan [[Shinzo Abe|Shinzō Abe]] and daughter of Prime Minister [[Nobusuke Kishi]].<ref>[https://giornalesm.com/266285/ San Marino. Sarà inaugurato questa mattina alle 10.30 al podere Lesignano, il San Marino Jinja]</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2014-06-22 |title=Un tempio shintoista a San Marino. E' il primo ufficiale in Europa |url=https://www.ilrestodelcarlino.it/rimini/cronaca/2014/06/22/1082095-san-marino-tempio-shintoista.shtml |website=Il resto del Carlino |language=it}}</ref> The shrine was established at the initiative of the [[Japan San Marino Friendship Society]] (JSFS) in commemoration of the victims of the [[2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami]].<ref>{{cite web |author=Stefano Carrer |date=2014-05-25 |title=Shintoisti a San Marino |url=https://st.ilsole24ore.com/art/notizie/2014-05-25/shintoisti-san-marino-081510.shtml |access-date=2023-09-13 |website=Il Sole 24 ORE |language=it}}</ref>

The Association of Shinto Shrines considers San Marino Jinja as the first official shrine in Europe.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Adnkronos |date=2020-12-19 |title=A San Marino il primo tempio shintoista d'Europa |url=https://www.adnkronos.com/Archivio/cronaca/a-san-marino-il-primo-tempio-shintoista-deuropa_4qNrQp88SXCpdZ7Odistcj |access-date=2024-01-21 |website=Adnkronos}}</ref>
However, as not all shrines fall under Association, the "Yamakage Shinto Holland Saigu" in The Netherlands, established in 1980 by the Japanese Dutch Shinzen Foundation, is actually the first jinja in Europe.<ref>Noriyoshi Tamaru and David Reid, Religion in Japanese Culture, Where Living Traditions Meet a Changing World, Kodansha International, 1996, p. 187</ref>

From 2019, marriages recognized by the Civil Registry office of the Republic of San Marino can be celebrated there, therefore valid throughout the world.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cerimonie ed eventi |url=https://www.sanmarinojinja.com/cerimonie/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201129095417/https://www.sanmarinojinja.com/cerimonie/ |url-status=usurped |archive-date=November 29, 2020 |access-date=2024-01-21 |website=San Marino Jinja |language=it-IT}}</ref>

== Main shrine ==
[[File:San Marino Jinja.jpg|left|thumb|200x200px|The sanctuary of San Marino with the ''tōrō'' (stone lanterns) at its entrance.]]
The style of the main hall is {{transliteration|ja|[[shinmei-zukuri]]}}, the same as that of the [[Ise Jingu]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=http://www.sanmarinoworld.com/?id=32&id_n=16735 |title=Un inno alla pace. Il tempio shinto a Lesignano è dedicato alle vittime del terremoto del 2011 |access-date=2024-01-21 |archive-date=2016-03-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304142801/http://www.sanmarinoworld.com/?id=32&id_n=16735 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In the shrine area there are also a {{transliteration|ja|torii}} (portal), a pair of {{transliteration|ja|[[tōrō]]}} (lanterns) and a small {{transliteration|ja|[[chōzuya]]}} ([[Ritual purification#Shinto|ablution]] fountain), all very frequent elements in Shinto architecture.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Shintoisti a San Marino |url=http://www.ilsole24ore.com/art/notizie/2014-05-25/shintoisti-san-marino-081510.shtml?uuid=ABCzyxKB |access-date=2024-01-21 |website=Il Sole 24 ORE |language=it}}</ref> The shine of San Marino consists of a small square-based monument with a side of 2.5 meters and made in Japan with cedar wood. Parts of the main hall were built using wood from the Ise Jingu shrine.

The main hall was built in Japan, dismantled and transported by sea to San Marino, where it was rebuilt by Japanese architects on a foundation made of typical sandstone.

The temple is surrounded by numerous rows of [[vine]]s, set against the backdrop of the Mediterranean mountains and landscapes.

== Deities ==
The Shrine of San Marino is consecrated to the kami [[Amaterasu]], the personification of the Sun, the primary source of life on Earth. She is thus the most important deity of the Shinto pantheon, as she is also a traditional ancestor of [[Emperor of Japan|Japanese emperors]]. starting with the legendary [[Emperor Jimmu|Jimmu]], her great-grandson.

== Shinto priest ==
[[File:Guji Francesco Brigante.jpg|thumb|Chief priest Francesco Brigante performs a Shinto ritual at San Marino Shrine (2016)]]
The {{transliteration|ja|[[miyazukasa]]}} (chief Shinto priest) of the San Marino Shrine is {{nihongo|Francesco Brigante|フランチェスコ・ブリガンテ|Furanchesuko Burigante}}, who received his Shinto priesthood status from the Shinto Shrine Honcho and was appointed as chief priest in 2013 and awarded the {{transliteration|ja|[[bushidō]]}} honour. He is a local San Marino hotel owner who trained at [[Yudonosan Shrine]] in [[Yamagata Prefecture]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-11-09 |title=実はヨーロッパに輸出されている日本の神社｜東條英利コラム - デイリーニュースオンライン |url=https://dailynewsonline.jp/article/897140/ |access-date=2024-01-21 |website=dailynewsonline.jp |language=ja}}</ref>

Currently, the shrine is headed by Yoshiki Jinguji, who obtained his priesthood qualification to serve the San Marino Shrine at the [[Dewa Shrine|Dewa Sanzan Shrine]] (Mt. Haguro) priesthood training school, also in [[Tsuruoka City]], Yamagata Prefecture.
